title: Motives of belief feed faith, but they are not its chief certainty
source_text: XXXII. Attamen non existimamus argumenta illa et credendi motiva, quibus verbum Dei suadetur, et quibus hominum mentes leniter ad ejus obsequium flectuntur, esse illud unde fidei certitudo potissimum pendet, et praecipuum illius fundamentum. His quidem argumentis Deus utitur in fide generanda, et iis quoque fides jam generata alitur et fovetur: non tamen videntur esse fidei potissima basis et certitudinis illius mensura. Et hoc quia, ut jam thesi 8. dictum, consentiunt scholae Christianae certitudinem fidei summam esse, et talem quae vel aequet, vel etiam superet, certitudinem omnem quae reperitur in scientiis humanis, nempe, si fides aestimetur ex suis principiis et consideretur qualis esse potest, et debet: non autem qualis revera sit in multis. Sed fides qua verbum Dei, quod hodie Scriptura continetur, suscipimus, non potest habere illam certitudinem, si nitatur tantum notis et argumentis, quibus Scriptura divina comprobatur. Nec enim sunt demonstrationes quae certitudinem absolutam generent, sed argumenta solum moralia, quae, licet sufficiant ut aliquis ad prudenter credendum inducatur, non tamen per se, et ex sua natura, possunt gignere certitudinem parem illi quam habent, verbi causa, disciplinae Mathematicae: qualem aut etiam majorem supponimus fidem acquirere.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless we do not judge that those arguments and motives of believing by which God's Word is recommended, and by which people's minds are gently bent toward obedience to it, are that from which the certainty of faith chiefly hangs, and its principal foundation. God does use these arguments in generating faith, and by them also faith already generated is nourished and fostered; yet they do not seem to be faith's strongest basis and the measure of its certainty. And this is because, as already said in thesis 8, the Christian schools agree that the certainty of faith is the highest, and such that it either equals or even surpasses every certainty found in the human sciences — namely if faith is estimated from its own principles and considered as it can and ought to be, not as it actually is in many people. But the faith by which we receive God's Word as it is contained today in Scripture cannot have that certainty if it rests only on the notes and arguments by which Scripture is proved divine. For they are not demonstrations that generate absolute certainty, but only moral arguments which, though they suffice to lead someone to believe prudently, cannot of themselves and by their nature produce a certainty equal to that which the mathematical disciplines have, for example — the kind of certainty, or even a greater one, that we suppose faith acquires.
pass_b_english: Still, we do not think those arguments and motives of belief — the ones that recommend God's Word and gently bend minds toward obedience to it — are what faith's certainty chiefly hangs on, or its principal foundation. God does use them when he generates faith, and by them faith already generated is also nourished and kept warm. They do not seem to be faith's strongest basis, or the measure of its certainty.

The Christian schools already agree on this, as thesis 8 said: faith's certainty is the highest — equal to every certainty in the human sciences, or even above them — when faith is judged from its own principles and taken as it can and ought to be, not as it actually stands in many people. But the faith that receives God's Word as Scripture now holds it cannot have that certainty if it rests only on the notes and arguments that prove Scripture divine. Those are not demonstrations that produce absolute certainty. They are only moral arguments. They can lead a person to believe prudently, yet by themselves and by their nature they cannot generate a certainty equal to what the mathematical disciplines have — the kind of certainty, or even a greater one, that we suppose faith acquires.

Keeps comparative force of potissima without inflating to sole basis.
